Show notes

  • This table always shows full, unfiltered totals for the current Report Period. Click a month, then a rep, to drill into individual leads. To filter by sales rep, meeting status, booked-via, and/or proposal status, use the Filter & Drill Into Leads section below, which breaks matching leads out separately without changing the totals here.
  • All proposal figures here (Call 2 Attended, Total Proposals Sent, Win Rate, Total Amount) come from the 44 proposals directly linked to a specific lead in "LEADS, MEETINGS, PROPOSALS.csv" — a real relationship, not name-matched. Show note

We don't track Call 2 attendance directly in Zoho, so per process: leads come in → booked in the system or booked by the sales rep → Call 1 → Call 2 is scheduled but not tracked. Every lead with a real Attendance Status (Attended/No Show/Canceled/Upcoming) in "LEADS, MEETINGS, PROPOSALS.csv" counts toward Call 1 — 292 of the 1,533 total leads for this period — and a lead is assumed to have attended Call 2 if a proposal was created for them. Each is attributed to the rep who actually hosted the meeting (the Host column), which is occasionally different from the lead's current Owner since ownership reverts to "Jenni Mize" (intake/admin) once a lead goes inactive. 6 meetings were hosted by Jenni Mize herself rather than a named rep; they show under "All Reps" and in the "Jenni Mize" line of the Call 2 rep breakdown, but won't appear if you filter to a single named rep. Filter by sales rep, attendance status, how the call was booked (In System / Sales Rep), and/or proposal status — every total and percentage in the table below recalculates for whatever combination of filters is active. Proposal Status matches a lead if any of their proposals has that stage. Total Proposals Sent, Win Rate, and Total Amount are all built from these same 44 lead-linked proposals (36 originally, plus 7 more leads/9 proposals reconstructed Aug 4, 2026 from Client records and Cassie's confirmed dates, with later confirmed exclusions and newly added leads bringing the total to 41 as of the Aug 10, 2026 refresh, then to 43 on Aug 15, 2026 once Chris Husted’s 2 DENmaar Inc proposals were confirmed genuinely connected, then to 44 on Aug 22, 2026 once Above And Beyond Transportation - CAS was confirmed genuinely connected to Darius Brown, an 8th reconstructed lead) — of everyone in our 2026 lead list, only 44 proposals can actually be traced back to a specific lead, so that's the number this table (and its rep/lead drill-down) uses throughout. A separate, fuller export tags 56 proposals as genuinely Facebook-sourced in 2026 overall (5 more were in the original 59-row export but confirmed by Cassie to be non-Facebook-sourced and excluded from every total on this dashboard), shown in "Proposals by Sales Rep & Status" and "Proposals 2026 by Month & Status" below for reference, but those extra ~12 can't be tied back to a specific 2026 lead here — all 12 are now tracked as leads on the 2025 tab instead, since their real origin predates 2026. Then click a month to see the rep breakdown, and a rep to see the individual leads.

Show notes
  • Total Leads (Facebook): all Facebook leads generated that month (1,533 total); doesn't respond to any filters (no per-lead data at this level).
  • Total Meetings: every booked lead that month, any attendance status.
  • Lead → Meeting %: Total Meetings ÷ Total Leads (Facebook) — anchored to the unfiltered lead count, so filters only narrow the numerator.
  • Call 1 Attended / Show Rate %: narrows Total Meetings to just "Attended" status.
  • Call 2 Attended (Assumed): per-lead yes/no based on at least one proposal — an assumption, not a tracked status.
  • Call 1 → Call 2 %: Call 2 Attended ÷ Call 1 Attended (directional, not exact).
  • Total Proposals Sent: full proposal universe for the month (41 total), filterable by sales rep.
  • Win Rate: Closed Won ÷ Total Proposals Sent, within whatever proposal population the filters above have narrowed to.
  • Total Amount: sum of dollar value ($ Billed Annually) across every proposal counted in Total Proposals Sent that month.
  • In System / Sales Rep / Not Booked (Booking Source): split of Total Meetings by original booking method, now shown as 3 separate columns; a few conflicts were resolved by Created Time matching or direct confirmation from Cassie.
Show note

"Total Leads (Facebook)" is every Facebook lead generated that month (1,533 total, Jan – Aug 2026), regardless of whether they ever booked a call — a much broader pool than the columns to its right. It does NOT respond to any of the filters above, since this is a coarse monthly rollup with no per-lead rep/status/booking data to filter by. "Total Meetings" is every booked lead that month, counted as Call 1 regardless of recorded attendance status (Attended/No Show/Canceled/Upcoming). "Lead → Meeting %" = Total Meetings ÷ Total Leads (Facebook), i.e. what share of that month’s Facebook leads ever got a call booked at all. It’s anchored to the unfiltered Total Leads (Facebook) figure, so only its numerator (Total Meetings) narrows when you apply the Sales Rep/Meeting Status/Booked Via/Proposal Status filters — treat filtered views of this rate as directional. "Call 1 Attended" and "Call 1 Show Rate %" narrow that down to leads with a recorded "Attended" status specifically. "Call 2 Attended" is a per-lead yes/no (at least one proposal), not a proposal count. "Call 1 → Call 2 %" = Call 2 Attended ÷ Call 1 Attended, so it measures conversion among leads who actually showed up to Call 1 — not the full Total Meetings pool. This is an assumption, not a directly tracked status, so treat it as directional rather than exact. "Total Proposals Sent" is the full proposal universe for that month (41 total, proposal-level) and responds to the Sales Rep filter above like the other columns. "Win Rate" = Closed Won ÷ Total Proposals Sent, computed within whatever proposal population the Sales Rep/Booked Via/Proposal Status filters have already narrowed to — filtering to a single non-Won status will show 0% by design. "Total Amount" is the sum of dollar value (Sum of Billed Annually) across every proposal counted in that month’s Total Proposals Sent figure, so it moves together with that column under the same filters. "Booking Source" (In System / Sales Rep / Not Booked) is a count split of Total Meetings by how the call was originally booked — "FB Calendly Appt" = Yes (In System) vs. a rep booking it directly (Sales Rep) vs. neither being determinable (Not Booked) — now read straight from each lead's own FB Calendly Appt field in "LEADS, MEETINGS, PROPOSALS.csv," since that export joins booking, meeting, and proposal data per lead in one place (no more cross-referencing separate exports by name). Shown as 3 separate columns rather than one combined "X / Y" figure, to avoid the "/" reading like a ratio.

Show note

This table mirrors the 2026 Lead Conversion Data table's columns. "LEAD AND MEETING 2025.csv" supplies each lead's real Created Time (May – Dec 2025, 1,805 leads — this source doesn't cover Jan – Apr 2025, which appears to predate this ad campaign's Facebook lead flow), meeting Host, and a genuine Attendance Status field (Attended/No Show/Canceled/Upcoming) for each of its 384 booked meetings — so Call 1 Attended and Call 1 Show Rate below are measured the same way as the 2026 tab, not assumed. "Facebook Leads - Proposals (3).csv" is a Zoho export with real Proposals Owner and dollar amount (Billed Annually) per proposal — a big upgrade over the earlier Ignition-based proposals file, which had neither. That export spans May 2025 – Jul 2026 (148 rows); only its 92 rows dated in 2025 are used here. Unlike the 2026 table, which links each proposal to a specific lead and can therefore group by that lead's own creation month (a true cohort view: closed regardless of when), these 2025 proposals have no lead reference at all — we checked, and their client names don't match any name in our 2025 Facebook lead export, most likely because a lead converts out of the Lead module once it closes and drops off lead exports pulled afterward. So "Total Proposals Sent," "Win Rate," and "Total Amount" here are bucketed by each proposal's own Created Time month, independent of any lead's cohort. "Call 2 Attended (Assumed)" is the count of unique clients with at least one proposal that month (deduped by the proposal's own Client Name field, per Cassie's direction on Aug 6, 2026 — a client with 2–3 proposals the same month, like Wendy Rose or Denise Gitsham, now only counts once), not a raw proposal count, and "Call 1 → Call 2 %" divides that unique count by Call 1 Attended. It's still not a verified per-lead link (we can't confirm this specific client is the same person who attended Call 1), so treat it as directional — but it's a real improvement over just echoing the proposal count. For the exact Signed/Lost/Sent date of any individual proposal — including ones created in one year but closed in another — see "Proposals 2025 by Month & Status" further down the page. Booking Source (In System / Sales Rep / Not Booked) uses the FB Calendly Appt field the same way as 2026, now shown as 3 separate columns instead of one combined "X / Y" figure. Total Leads (Facebook) always shows the full raw monthly count and doesn't respond to these filters, matching how the 2026 table's Total Leads column behaves.

Insights

  • 1
    These two campaigns aren't playing the same game
    Quantity Ad's $185 cost per booked call looks 4x cheaper than Quality Ad's $759 — but Quantity Ad fills a lead form while Quality Ad books the call directly. Different jobs, so the comparison table above isn't apples-to-apples.
  • 2
    The single highest-leverage move is on the Quantity Ad side
    "Case Studies" is a proven ~9.7x-return ad running at a fraction of its usual budget. See the Quantity Ad tab for the full story.

Observations (why results look weaker even as spend holds up)

Show note

Both campaigns are set to the same $300/day budget cap — so "budget" here means actual daily spend against that cap, not the cap itself.

▲

Quantity Ad stopped spending its own daily budget

Both campaigns share an identical $300/day cap. That makes this less a story about money moving between campaigns, and more about one campaign no longer spending the budget it's already allowed.

Ruled Out
Either campaign's budget cap was cut

Both are still set to $300/day — that setting hasn't changed. Whatever's happening, it isn't a deliberate reallocation between campaigns.

Confirmed
Quantity Ad's actual delivery has collapsed

It spent 99.6–99.8% of its $300/day cap (~$299/day) in April and May. In July, that fell to just 38.1% (~$114/day) — a real drop in delivery against an unchanged budget.

Most Likely Driver
The CPM spike is making its own budget harder to spend

Quantity Ad's CPM jumped 72% from March to June (see the Quantity Ad tab). At pricier auctions, the same bid settings win fewer auctions per dollar — which shows up exactly as reduced daily spend, even though the $300/day cap never changed. Quality Ad's July jump, meanwhile, is unrelated: it launched Jun 29, so June was just 2 partial days ($288/day, already near its own cap); by July it's simply running a full month at ~95% of its own $300/day budget — normal ramp-up, not evidence of money being pulled from Quantity Ad.

In short: this isn't a reallocation problem — it's a delivery problem. Fixing Quantity Ad means finding out why it can't spend the $300/day it's already budgeted for (likely a bid-strategy/CPM issue), not increasing its budget further.

Next Steps

  • 1
    Fix Quantity Ad's delivery, not its budget
    Top priority — it's already set to the same $300/day cap as Quality Ad but is only spending ~38% of it. Details on the Quantity Ad tab.
  • 2
    Fix the post-click funnel on both campaigns
    Different problems on each side — see the Quantity Ad and Quality Ad tabs for specifics.
  • 3
    With a limited budget, fund Quantity Ad before Quality Ad
    "Case Studies" is cheaper per lead (~$50–58) and has a proven track record; Quality Ad's best ad still needs ~$469 spent for one likely booked call. If dollars are tight, put them on Quantity Ad first and hold Quality Ad's spend until there's enough budget for a real, dedicated test.

Insights

Show note

Combines the firm's internal Meta ad/CRM report (historical context, pulled Jul 21, 2026) with the current ad-platform export above (source of truth, through Jul 30, 2026).

  • 1
    Win rate is the real opportunity, not lead volume
    70 deals closed won for $1.14M against $116K in ad spend (~9.7x return) — but 64 deals worth nearly as much ($1.12M) were lost. Closing more of what's already coming in beats generating more leads.
  • 2
    The lead decline is a CPM problem, not fatigue
    CTR improved and frequency dropped through 2026, ruling out ad fatigue and audience saturation. CPM jumped 72% (Mar $62 → Jun $107), buying 31–41% fewer impressions for the same spend.
  • 3
    Click → booked call is the biggest leak in the funnel
    Only 2.78% of this campaign's 22,968 link clicks turned into a booked call — a bigger gap than CPM or CTR. The form's qualification step and landing page are the highest-leverage fix.
  • 4
    "Case Studies" has been a single point of failure for over a year
    One ad has carried 94–98% of this campaign's spend, leads, and booked calls since launch. It's proven, but nothing else was ever given a real, funded test alongside it.
  • 5
    Wasn't fully paused — it just isn't spending its own budget
    An earlier historical report flagged this campaign as paused since late June. The current export (through Jul 30) shows it's still live and spending $3,432 in July — but that's only ~$114/day against its unchanged $300/day cap (38% utilization), down from ~99% in April/May. It's under-delivering, not off.
  • 6
    The June creative test never got a fair shot
    "Section 162" and 9 other new ads launched just 3 weeks before spend dropped off — not enough runway to know if any of them could beat "Case Studies."

Observations (why lead volume actually declined)

▲

Lead volume has been sliding since February

Leads peaked at 284 in January 2026, then fell — and spend held steady at $8–9.3K/month through that stretch, so this isn't a budget pullback. The same money bought fewer leads. Testing the "Case Studies" ad's own month-by-month numbers against three explanations points fairly clearly at one of them.

Ruled Out
Creative fatigue

Fatigue shows up as CTR falling as the audience tires of the ad. CTR actually improved — 1.36% in March up to 1.95–2.19% in May/June. The creative isn't the problem.

Ruled Out
Audience saturation

Saturation shows up as frequency climbing while reach flattens. Frequency actually dropped — 2.06 in March down to 1.22 in June. The audience isn't tapped out.

Doesn't Fully Hold
Seasonal dip

May–Jun 2025 CPM was $56–63. May–Jun 2026 CPM was $104–107 — nearly double, for the same calendar months. If this were just tax season winding down the same way it did last year, CPM shouldn't be this different year over year.

Most Likely Driver
CPM spike

CPM jumped 72% from March ($61.93) to June ($106.66). With spend roughly flat, that bought 31–41% fewer impressions — and fewer impressions is the whole reason fewer leads came in, even though the ad itself performed as well as ever.

In short: this looks like rising cost-per-impression in the auction, not a problem with the ad or the audience — which is exactly why the fix is budget, not new creative.

Next Steps

  • 1
    Find out why "Case Studies" isn't spending its own $300/day budget
    Its budget cap hasn't changed — it's spending only ~$114/day (38%) against the same $300/day cap it used to fully spend. Check Ads Manager for delivery issues (learning-phase reset, bid cap too low for the higher CPM, audience/frequency limits) rather than assuming it needs more money.
  • 2
    Fix the post-click funnel
    Audit the on-form qualification question and the landing/calendar page — that's where 97%+ of clicks are being lost, not in the ad itself.
  • 3
    Push for a higher proposal win rate
    Closed Lost ($1.12M) is almost as large as Closed Won ($1.14M) — a modest close-rate lift beats most volume-side fixes.
  • 4
    Give "Section 162" (or any new creative) a real runway
    4–6 weeks and dedicated budget — not 2–3 weeks squeezed in before spend drops off.
  • 5
    Track CPM monthly, not just spend and leads
    The CPM spike was visible as early as April but wasn't flagged until leads had fallen for three straight months.

Insights

  • 1
    "Still Ad - 2" is the proven performer
    It's driven 6 of this campaign's 12 total booked calls — half of everything — and its results have held up as spend increased, unlike some of the other ads here.
  • 2
    "Video Ad - 1" looked like a winner early, but it didn't hold up
    Through mid-July it had the cheapest cost per booked call in the campaign on just 2 conversions. By month end, another $1,425 in spend produced zero additional booked calls — a small-sample fluke, not a real trend.
  • 3
    This campaign is brand new — treat everything here as directional
    Only 2 months and 12 total booked calls of data exist so far. Spend scaled roughly 15x from June to July, and cost per booked call still rose despite the media itself getting cheaper — see the observation below for why.

Observations (why cost per booked call rose anyway)

▲

Cost per booked call rose even though the media got cheaper

Between June and July, spend scaled 14.8x ($577 → $8,526) as this campaign ramped up. Cost per booked call still rose over the same stretch, from $577 to $775 — worth checking why, since CPM and CTR both actually moved in the right direction.

Ruled Out
Rising CPM

CPM actually fell from $119.27 in June to $78.89 in July as spend scaled up — buying media got cheaper, not pricier.

Ruled Out
Falling CTR

CTR improved from 2.30% to 2.88%. Cost per click roughly halved, from $5.19 to $2.74 — clicks got cheaper and more plentiful.

Doesn't Fully Hold
Audience saturation

Frequency rose only from 1.16 to 1.52 — still low for a "Broad" audience, nowhere near the saturation levels seen elsewhere in the account.

Most Likely Driver
Click → booked-call rate collapsed

That rate fell from 0.90% of clicks in June to just 0.35% in July, even as click volume grew nearly 28x. The extra volume brought in clicks that convert far less often — the same click→booked-call leak flagged on the Quantity Ad side, showing up here as this campaign scales.

In short: buying clicks got cheaper and more efficient as this campaign scaled, but turning those clicks into booked calls didn't scale with it — the bottleneck is downstream, on the landing/booking page itself, not in the media buy.

Next Steps

  • 1
    Keep budget behind "Still Ad - 2"
    It's the clear, sustained performer — consider briefing 1–2 new creatives built on whatever's working about it (hook, format, offer angle).
  • 2
    Don't over-invest in "Video Ad - 1" yet
    Its early efficiency was a 2-conversion sample that didn't hold up with more spend.
  • 3
    Keep scaling, but watch cost per booked call closely each month
    12 total conversions is too small to extrapolate confidently — revisit after another 4–6 weeks of data.
  • 4
    Check the booking page directly
    This funnel skips the lead form entirely — whatever's holding back bookings is happening on that one landing/booking page, which makes it the easier of the two campaigns to test and fix.

▲

First closed win has landed; volume still climbing, still early to call performance

In its first 39 days of paid ad data (Aug 14–Sep 21, 2026), Aruga Digital spent $11,492.24 across the two campaigns and generated 227 Zoho-tracked, campaign-tagged leads as of the Sep 22, 2026 refresh — 126 through the existing "Book a Call Funnel" campaign and 101 through the "Instant Forms" campaign. Meta's own attribution shows 234 form-fill results and 43 booked calls ($267.26 cost per booked call) over the ad-spend window, which lines up closely with the 52 of 227 tagged leads that show a booked meeting in Zoho (18 Attended, 16 Upcoming, 16 No Show, 2 Canceled) — a good sign that Meta's and Zoho's counts are still tracking together as this campaign scales up.

"Instant Forms" is a genuinely new lead-gen format (on-platform instant forms rather than a landing-page click-through), so its $54.73 cost per lead-form result and 17 booked calls so far are still a growing sample, not a verdict. The continuing "Book a Call Funnel" campaign ($5,745.78 spend, 129 results, 26 booked, $44.54 cost/result) is the same campaign flagged on the Quantity Ad tab for under-spending its budget and losing clicks after the click — worth watching whether Aruga's management changes either of those patterns as more weeks of data come in. The closing-time boxes above now show two real data points — the "Book a Call Funnel" lead (tagged Aug 25) that reached two proposals on Sep 2, one already Closed Lost, and a second "Book a Call Funnel" lead (tagged Aug 30) that closed a $547 proposal Closed Won on Sep 8 — still an early sample, but the first confirmed win directly tied to Aruga's management.

NPS Report

Net Promoter Score, from the client survey sent via Zoho Survey. Currently reflects Jul 2026, the first month tracked on this dashboard — future months will be added here as new survey exports come in.

Overview

Show description

Every respondent rates “how likely are you to recommend Peter Holtz CPA to a friend or colleague” on a 0–10 scale. Scores of 9–10 are Promoters, 7–8 are Passives, and 0–6 are Detractors. NPS score = % Promoters − % Detractors, so it ranges from −100 to +100.

Feedback Themes (Jul 2026)

▲

Communication is the dominant complaint behind the low score

Of the 9 respondents who left written feedback, 7 specifically called out slow, unclear, or one-sided communication — not the quality of the tax/accounting work itself.

Most Likely Driver
Clients have to chase updates themselves

Recurring language: replies take “days to weeks,” clients have “had to ask multiple times for updates,” and one account changed hands ~4 times in a year with no continuity. This points to a proactive-update gap rather than a one-off staffing issue.

Separate Theme
Unresolved issues, not just slow replies

Two of the lowest scores (0 and 1) cite open items that were never actually closed out — a wage garnishment the client says was never addressed, and general items still “pending.” This is a follow-through problem on top of the communication one.

What's working: only two respondents left an explicitly positive comment — see the banner above — praising consistency and the combined bookkeeping/CPA offering. The other 4 of 5 Promoters (scores 9–10) left no comment at all, suggesting nothing stood out enough to mention, good or bad.
